newsitem.title: USA: Merrill never involved in yield burning - spokesman.
newsitem.headline: Merrill never involved in yield burning - spokesman.

text.p: A spokesman for Merrill Lynch & Co said the firm did not deceive state and local governments by secretly inflating prices on the U.S. Treasuries they sold them.
"Merrill has never been involved in yield burning and all of the transactions we've undertaken for issuers have been proper and professional," the spokesman said in a telephone interview.
And the firm has never been lead manager for any refunding for the Los Angeles Country Metroplitan Transportation Authority, the spokesman said.

The authority charged in written comments to the Internal Revenue Service on Tuesday that localities were "exploited and deceived" by Wall Street firms that "knowingly" inflated prices on escrow securities above fair market value.

The county offered an analysis by Boston consulting firm Michel/Shaked Group, which priced 104 advance refunding escrow deals and concluded that on average, noncompetitive deals had "unjustified markups" of about $4 per $1,000 per bond.

The study said the top two senior managers of negotiated advance refundings would have made a total of $186 million in yield burning profits, in what drafters of the L.A. comments called a conservative estimate.
The comment letter did not name the two firms. However, Securities Data Co., an industry data collector, said the top two underwriters were Goldman, Sachs & Co. and Merrill.
But Merrill's spokesman said that senior managers of negotiated advance refundings are "not necessarily involved with the structure and purchase of escrow securities."

Thus, said one industry observer, it is impossible to look at rankings of bond refunding issuance and conclude "how much of that universe actually involved the purchase of securities for escrows by the senior manager."
"It's quite conceivable that the firm that was number five in refunding rankings could have done more escrows than the number one firm," said the observer, who asked not to be identified.

The $1.3 trillion municipal bond market has been rocked by allegations that bond underwriters overcharge issuers for U.S. Treasuries bought in the open market and used in bond financing transactions, a practice called "yield burning."

The Internal Revenue Service in July shocked muncipalities nationwide by announcing that localities that paid more than fair market value for Treasuries can enter into "closing agreements" with IRS to avoid having interest on their bonds declared taxable.
Meanwhile, a Goldman spokesman said this week, "We believe that any actions the firm took on behalf of isuers are proper and legal."
